To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
atropine inhibits cold air-induced bronchospasm in a dose-dependent manner.

the bronchomotion response to cold air is vagally mediated, and that higher doses are needed to block the response to cold air than those needed to block the effect of a large dose (1.0%) of methacholine.

atropine inhibits the bronchoconstriction produced by cold air in a dose-dependent manner and that the dose of atropin required to inhibit this response depends on the degree of bronchoconstriction caused by cold air after a placebo inhalation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of atropine in a dose-dependent manner.
the effects of atropine in doses that do not affect base-line sRaw.
the effect of cold dry air on the airways.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the dose-dependent effect of atropine in inhibiting cold air-induced bronchospasm is a function of the dose of atropin and the magnitude of the bronchial response to cold air, which in turn is a function of baseline airway reactivity.
the effect of cold on the bronchomotricity is mediated through vagal pathways.
the effect of cold on airway tone is not mediated by vagal cholinergic mechanisms.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the bronchoconstriction caused by cold air is vagally mediated but that higher doses of atropin are required to inhibit this response than are required to reduce base line bronchomotor tone or to inhibit bronchomotor responses to an inhaled muscarninic agent.
atropine is a useful drug to use in asthma.
atropine in doses greater than or equal to 0.26 micrograms/kg body weight inhibits bronchoconstriction caused by cold air in a dose-dependent manner.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the vagal pathway may be important in the bronchoconstriction induced by exposure to cold air, but that this effect is not as easily blocked by antimuscarinic therapy as are the effects of inhaled bronchoconstrictor drugs.

cold air can cause bronchoconstriction and that this response can be inhibited by atropine, but higher doses of atropin are required to inhibit cold air-induced airway constriction than to reduce base-line sRaw or to inhibit the bronchial response to a large dose of inhaled methacholine.
cold air can cause bronchoconstriction via vagally-mediated pathways.
